**Clayton Lee Waagner** (born August 25, 1956) is an American convicted [bank robber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_robber "Bank robber") and [anti-abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-abortion "Anti-abortion") [terrorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorist "Terrorist"). He was born **Roger Waagner** in [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota"). He was an escaped [fugitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fugitive "Fugitive") during the spring, summer and fall of 2001 and was the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI "FBI")'s [467th fugitive to be placed on the Ten Most Wanted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s "FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives, 2000s") list for carjackings, firearms violations, and bank robbery on September 21, 2001. He was placed on the [United States Marshals Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marshals_Service "United States Marshals Service") Top 15 Fugitives list for sending more than 280 letters that claimed to contain [anthrax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthrax "Anthrax"), which he mailed to [Planned Parenthood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood "Planned Parenthood") with return addresses of the Marshals Service and the [Secret Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secret_Service "United States Secret Service") beginning in October 2001.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He is currently in prison.

## Prior crimes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Waagner&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Prior crimes")]

Waagner had previously been sentenced to 4–10 years for attempted robbery in 1992. Years later as a convicted felon released from prison, early in September 1999, he was pulled over by the [Pennsylvania State Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_Police "Pennsylvania State Police"), but fled into the woods and evaded capture, leaving behind a stolen car that contained firearms, explosives, [false identity papers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_document_forgery "Identity document forgery"), and a list of [abortion clinics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_clinic "Abortion clinic").

Later in September 1999, while on a self-described "mission from [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God "God")", he took his wife and their nine children on a cross-country road trip headed west in a stolen [Winnebago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnebago_Industries "Winnebago Industries"), planning to [murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder "Murder") various abortion doctors, beginning with one in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"), [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state) "Washington (state)"). However, after crossing into [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois") his vehicle broke down, and Waagner was arrested when [Illinois State Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_State_Police "Illinois State Police") stopped to investigate. Waagner was convicted on charges of interstate transportation of a stolen motor vehicle and for being a convicted [felon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felony "Felony") in possession of [firearms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firearm "Firearm").

While he was awaiting sentencing and facing a term of 15 years to life, Waagner escaped from [DeWitt County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeWitt_County,_Illinois "DeWitt County, Illinois") Jail in [Clinton, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton,_Illinois "Clinton, Illinois"), on February 22, 2001.

## Escaped fugitive crime trail

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Waagner&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Escaped fugitive crime trail")]

As an escaped fugitive felon from Clinton, Illinois, Waagner made his way back east to Pennsylvania, where three months later he became wanted for the bank robbery of a [First Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Union "First Union") in [Harrisburg, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrisburg,_Pennsylvania "Harrisburg, Pennsylvania") in May 2001.

His fugitive trail then led southwest, where he was next identified as having abandoned a vehicle in [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"), following a hit and run accident. Authorities recovered law enforcement-type equipment, anti-abortion literature, and weapons from the car. He next became wanted for [carjackings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carjacking "Carjacking") across the state line in [Tunica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunica,_Mississippi "Tunica, Mississippi"), and [Robinsonville, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinsonville,_Mississippi "Robinsonville, Mississippi"), and firearms violations in [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"), on September 7, 2001. Later that month, the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") placed him on the [list of Ten Most Wanted Fugitives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives "FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives"), in the wake of the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

## Anthrax hoax

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Waagner&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Anthrax hoax")]

See also: [Anthrax hoaxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthrax_hoaxes "Anthrax hoaxes")

Waagner's eventual notoriety is largely attributable to the [hoax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoax "Hoax") he then perpetrated in November 2001, in which he sent envelopes containing a white powder to more than 500 [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion "Abortion") providers. From the [Army of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_God_(USA) "Army of God (USA)"), Virginia Dare Chapter". The threat was considered serious, as it arrived shortly after the September 11 terrorist attacks against the United States, as well as the then-recent [delivery of genuine anthrax letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_anthrax_attacks "2001 anthrax attacks") to various governmental officials. A [United States Marshals Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marshals_Service "United States Marshals Service") Top 15 Fugitive since March 6, 2001, Waagner also became an [FBI Ten Most Wanted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted "FBI Ten Most Wanted") fugitive because of the more than 280 letters that threatened to contain anthrax, which he mailed to [Planned Parenthood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood "Planned Parenthood"), with return addresses of the [U.S. Marshals Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Marshals_Service "U.S. Marshals Service") and the [U.S. Secret Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Secret_Service "U.S. Secret Service") beginning in October 2001. In the wave of mailed letters, Waagner was accused of stalkings and threats to kill 42 low-level [abortion clinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_clinic "Abortion clinic") employees up through November 23, 2001.

**PHILADELPHIA** - Assistant Attorney General for the Justice Departments
Civil Rights Division R. Alexander Acosta, U.S. Attorney Patrick L. Meehan and
Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Special Agent-in-Charge Jeffrey A.
Lampinski today announced a guilty verdict in a criminal civil rights case.

A federal jury found Clayton Lee Waagner guilty of making threats to employees
of reproductive clinics after a two-week trial. Waagner was convicted of
violating the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act, of interstate
transmission and mailing of threatening communications, and of threatening the
use of a weapon of mass destruction. He faces a maximum possible sentence of
life imprisonment.

"While many people of goodwill have deeply held views about abortion, the
Justice Department will prosecute those who cross the line from honestly held
beliefs to violent and unlawful actions," said Assistant Attorney General
Acosta. "We are pleased that the jury agreed that the defendant's actions here
crossed far past that line."

stating that he was going to escalate the war on abortionists. In this letter,
Waagner stated that "I am going to kill as many of them as I can. Waagner
proceeded to make numerous death threats to individuals who worked for womens
reproductive health care clinics.

Furthermore, Waagner sent hundreds of letters to reproductive health care
clinics throughout the eastern portion of the United States. The phrase, TIME
SENSITIVE SECURITY INFORMATION, OPEN IMMEDIATELY was typewritten on the
outside of many of the envelopes. The letters contained an unidentified powder
which was purported to be anthrax. Waagner mailed these threatening letters on
the heels of letters sent to Florida, Washington, D.C. and New Jersey that
actually contained anthrax spores and caused the illness and death of several
innocent people. While Waagner targeted abortion clinics, he also mistakenly
sent these "anthrax letters" to several pro-life organizations.

His threats to kill and injure were chilling, specific, and public, said
Meehan. He promised to deliver anthrax and other bio-weapons through the
mail. Our prosecution of this case clearly demonstrates that we take such
threats seriously and those who make them will be held accountable.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, as well as state and local law
enforcement agencies, investigated this matter. Assistant U.S. Attorney
Richard Barrett and Sheila Berman, trial attorney from the Criminal Section of
the Justice Departments Civil Rights Division, jointly prosecuted the case.

# Prosecutors want life term for Waagner \*\* Anti-abortion activist sent fake anthrax to clinics after 9-11.

### Share this:

![Author](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=85&d=mm&r=g)

Federal prosecutors are seeking a life sentence for Clayton Lee Waagner, calling him a terrorist for sending fake anthrax with threatening letters to hundreds of abortion clinics.

If prosecutors are successful in securing the life sentence — which is more common for murder defendants — he would not be eligible for parole.

Waagner, who has called himself an “anti-abortion extremist,” induced fear at women’s clinics across the eastern United States, including those in Quakertown, Norristown, Doylestown and Pottstown. He took advantage of the fear gripping the nation during the fall of 2001, when letters with real anthrax were sent to members of Congress and the news media.

“His method was cruel and calculated to inflict maximum damage on the victims and on our society,” prosecutors said in a memo outlining their sentencing recommendation.

Waagner was scheduled to be sentenced Friday, but the hearing was postponed as lawyers and judges tried to sort out the details of a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that could affect his sentence. The ruling, which came Thursday, struck down aspects of Washington state’s sentencing guidelines. His sentencing was rescheduled for Aug. 24.

In December, a federal jury convicted Waagner of charges stemming from his filling envelopes with flour or white insecticide. Enclosed letters told recipients that the powder was anthrax.

“You’ve ignored our warnings, so now you pay,” some letters said. “Enclosed you’ll find the real thing — anthrax, very high grade. Be careful not to bring any of the spores home to your children.”

At the time, he was on the run from police after escaping from a prison in Illinois. He was supposed to be serving 49 years for firearms and car-theft convictions.

In another letter, he acknowledged the difficulty of fighting abortion in the courts and legislatures. “This letter is to put you on notice of a new era in the battle to protect the pre-born child. We will fight you on the streets of America.”

Waagner’s hoax placed an even greater strain on the nation’s emergency response system at a time when it was already stretched thin after the Sept. 11 attacks.

Hazardous materials teams and other rescue workers responded to many of the clinics, some of which had to be closed for days. The FBI pulled dozens of agents off other counter-terrorism assignments.

During his trial, Waagner acted as his own lawyer. The prosecutors used Waagner’s own words from his closing argument to try to convince U.S. District Judge Anita Brody that she should impose a life sentence.

“It’s been clearly demonstrated that I am the anti-abortion extremist, a terrorist to the abortion industry,” the prosecutors quoted Waagner as saying. “There’s no question there that I terrorized these people any way I could … I did it systematically. I did it over a period of time. I worked as hard as I could to do that.”

In their sentencing memo, prosecutors Richard Barrett and Sheila Berman included letters from some of the victims. “This is a diabolical, conniving criminal who needs to be put away for a very long time,” wrote the president of a Planned Parenthood clinic in Alabama.

Another Planned Parenthood employee wrote, “I hate what he and his followers stand for and the anguish they cause. I hate that he forces us to fear going to work.”

A third letter from a victim expressed the apprehension she felt at the time that she might die from anthrax exposure and her son would be left without a mother. “I cannot put into words the fear and panic I experienced at the thought of my son being left alone.”

The prosecutors argued that Waagner’s actions fit the federal definition for a crime of terrorism, thus helping push Waagner into the sentencing range that requires life imprisonment. The definition involves an offense that “is calculated to influence or affect the conduct of government by intimidation or coercion or to retaliate against government.”

In a written response, lawyer Luis Ortiz, who assisted Waagner, maintained that Waagner’s crime does not meet that definition. Waagner admitted that he could not win the battle against abortion by fighting the government in the courts or legislatures, according to Ortiz, so Waagner tried scare tactics in the community.

“Clayton Waagner intended to influence not the government, but the conduct of reproductive nonprofit clinics, namely Planned Parenthood,” Ortiz wrote.

Waagner was convicted of 51 counts of mailing threatening communications, interstate communication of threats and threatening to use a weapon of mass destruction.

# United States of America, Plaintiff-appellee, v. Clayton L. Waagner, Defendant-appellant, 319 F.3d 962 (7th Cir. 2003)

**Court:**U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit

**Citation:**319 F.3d 962

**Date Decided:**February 19, 2003

**U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit - 319 F.3d 962 (7th Cir. 2003)**

**Argued September 17, 2002

Decided February 19, 2003**

* * *

Richard N. Cox, Eugene L. Miller (argued), Office of U.S. Attorney, Urbana Div., Urbana, IL, for Plaintiff-Appellee.

J. Steven Beckett, Carol A. Dison (argued), Beckett & Webber, Urbana, IL, for Defendant-Appellant.

Before COFFEY, EVANS, and WILLIAMS, Circuit Judges.

TERENCE T. EVANS, Circuit Judge.

* * *

Clayton L. Waagner says that after his daughter suffered a miscarriage, he heard a voice ask "how could [he] grieve so hard over this one when millions are killed, or murdered, every year." Waagner said the voice, which only he could hear, belonged to God and that it went on to say "I have called you to be my warrior and I want you to go to war against the abortion industry." Describing himself as a "warrior for pre-born children," Waagner embarked on what ultimately became a 2-year, cross-country crime spree. The spree included staking out abortion clinics, stealing a 4-wheel drive Yukon on which he logged 30,000 miles, stealing a Winnebago motor home, robbing gas stations, burglarizing residences, and even evading Pennsylvania state troopers after a high-speed chase. Waagner, a convicted felon, stole firearms during his burglaries, and he went to great lengths to avoid apprehension, going so far as downloading police frequencies from the Internet and storing them on a CD-ROM so he could monitor police movements on a scanner.

Waagner was eventually apprehended by an Illinois state trooper in September of 1999 and subsequently charged with a couple of federal offenses—possession of a firearm by a felon and possession of a stolen motor vehicle which crossed state lines. _See_ 18 U.S.C. § 922(g) (1) and 18 U.S.C. § 2313(a).

It is, of course, certainly not surprising that someone who claims to hear bizarre commands from God and then embarks on a massive crime spree has more than a few mental problems. And Waagner did. This became clear when he filed a notice of intent to raise an insanity defense to the charges against him. After filing his notice, the government requested a psychiatric examination, and Waagner was evaluated by Dr. Daniel S. Greenstein, a clinical psychologist whose diagnosis was adjustment disorder, delusional disorder grandiose type, and antisocial personality disorder. Dr. Greenstein testified at Waagner's trial that the diagnoses of adjustment disorder and antisocial personality disorder were not severe mental diseases or defects. However, he testified that Waagner's "delusional disorder grandiose type" is a severe mental disease and that he would not necessarily be able to appreciate the wrongfulness of his actions. The insanity defense primarily rested on this opinion, but the jury didn't buy it, as Waagner was convicted on both counts.

Despite his loss at the trial, Waagner proved to be a tough nut to crack: he escaped from the DeWitt County jail in Clinton, Illinois, where he was in custody awaiting sentencing. The escape led to 9 more months of freedom before he was arrested again in December of 2001.

Back in court, Waagner pled guilty to a charge of escape under 18 U.S.C. § 751(a). Later, he was sentenced on all three counts of conviction. The district judge found that Waagner was an armed career criminal who possessed firearms in connection with crimes of violence, that he obstructed justice by escaping and, finally, that he had not shown acceptance of responsibility for either the original charges or the escape. Based on these findings, Waagner was sentenced to 327 months imprisonment on the gun charge, 120 months on the stolen vehicle charge, and 37 months on the escape charge. The gun and stolen vehicle sentences were ordered to run concurrent, but the escape sentence was consecutive—resulting in a total sentence of 364 months.

On this appeal, Waagner seeks a new trial on the original charges. His argument rests on a claim that the jury clearly erred in concluding that he failed to meet his burden of proof on the insanity defense and that the court erred in failing to give the jury a requested instruction on the consequences that would flow from a finding of not guilty by reason of mental defect. Failing that, Waagner tacks on a trio of challenges to the sentence imposed by the district judge.

Waagner's first claim, that the jury clearly erred in failing to find him not guilty by reason of insanity, is an offshoot of a routine challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence argument. As we have noted, a defendant making an ordinary sufficiency challenge "faces a nearly insurmountable hurdle [in that we will] consider the evidence in the light most favorable to the Government, defer to the credibility determination of the jury, and overturn a verdict only when the record contains no evidence, regardless of how it is weighed, from which the jury could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt." _United States v. Szarwark_, 168 F.3d 993, 995 (7th Cir. 1999) (quoting _United States v. Moore_, 115 F.3d 1348, 1363 (7th Cir. 1997)).

In an insanity case, unlike a typical challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence, the defendant's burden is even greater. At trial, it is the defendant, not the government, that must carry the burden of proving insanity (which is an affirmative defense) by clear and convincing evidence. 18 U.S.C. § 17(b). Because, under 704(b) of the Federal Rules of Evidence, legal insanity is a question to be decided by the trier of fact, the finding here by the jury may not be disturbed unless it is clearly erroneous. _United States v. Reed_, 997 F.2d 332, 334 (7th Cir. 1993).

To succeed on an insanity defense, a defendant must prove that as the result of a severe mental disease or defect he was unable to appreciate the nature and quality or wrongfulness of his acts. 18 U.S.C. § 17(a). So the question becomes, what was the evidence the jury considered, and was it so one-sided that any decision except a finding of not guilty by reason of mental defect must be cast aside? We think not.

Dr. Greenstein offered the only expert opinion evidence in this case. But on cross-examination, the doctor testified that whether Waagner even had a delusional disorder was a very close call, made more difficult because it involved religious beliefs. He noted that a person would not necessarily be delusional simply because the person believed, based on strongly held religious beliefs, that killing abortion doctors was morally justified. Because it was a close call, Dr. Greenstein testified that he felt ethically obliged to err in favor of diagnosing Waagner with a delusional disorder. Plus, the doctor candidly acknowledged that on the same facts a different psychologist might come to a different conclusion.

Dr. Greenstein's equivocal testimony is not surprising given that none of the objective evidence pointed very strongly toward a finding that Waagner had a severe mental disorder. Likewise, the diagnosis was further drawn into question because Waagner, despite an extensive criminal record, had no recorded history of psychiatric illness.

**Nikolay Alekseyevich Soltys** (May 19, 1974 – February 13, 2002) was a Ukrainian [fugitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fugitive "Fugitive") charged by the [United States District Court for the Eastern District of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_Eastern_District_of_California "United States District Court for the Eastern District of California") in a [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") arrest warrant. The federal charges were for [unlawful flight to avoid prosecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unlawful_flight_to_avoid_prosecution "Unlawful flight to avoid prosecution") and there were California arrest warrants for six murders of his family members in and around the [Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento "Sacramento") area in August 2001.

## Background

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nikolay_Soltys&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Residents from Soltys' former hometown of [Shumsk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shumsk "Shumsk") in [Western Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Ukraine "Western Ukraine") described him as a [shoemaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoemaker "Shoemaker") with violent and unpredictable behavior.[[1]](#cite_note-Fox_News_August_26-1)

At the time, Shumsk was a small religious town with a population of 5,000 residents. The town had four churches: two [Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodoxy "Orthodoxy") churches from different branches, one [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") and one [Pentecostal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostalism "Pentecostalism"). Soltys and his parents belonged to the Pentecostal congregation. His parents joined a wave of Ukrainian religious population seeking refuge to the United States. Having successfully been granted [refugee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee "Refugee") status in the U.S. by the former [Immigration and Naturalization Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_and_Naturalization_Service "Immigration and Naturalization Service") (INS), his parents migrated to New York. Soltys was known to have had violent episodes towards his parents.[[2]](#cite_note-Fox_News_August_23-2)[[1]](#cite_note-Fox_News_August_26-1)

[ABC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_News_(United_States) "ABC News (United States)") reported that a newspaper from his homeland, the Kyiv daily *Fakty* (Facts), noted Soltys as being "abrupt" and sometimes violent prior to moving to the United States. He had arrived in the U.S. to be with his physically ailing father.[[3]](#cite_note-ABC_News_August_23-3)

The *Fakty* had apparently confirmed the 27-year-old refugee had a history of violence during an interview of Soltys' parents-in-law. They also denied that his rejection for enrollment into the Ukrainian military service was due to his mental instability. Instead, the relatives told the *Fakty* "What kept him out of the army was due to his [flat feet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_feet#Military_studies "Flat feet")."[[3]](#cite_note-ABC_News_August_23-3)

Igor Nakonechnyi, the father of Soltys' wife Lyuba, told *Fakty* that three years prior to the murders Soltys had attacked Lyuba with an ax that Soltys had stored in a closet "for self-defense." Lyuba telephoned her parents seeking help, frantically asking them to come help her "so he doesn't kill me", Nakonechnyi told *Fakty*. "We begged our daughter not to marry him," Nakonechnyi said. "She always listened and was respectful, but then for the first time in her life she went against her parents, firmly saying, 'We love one another and I am going to live with him.'" [[3]](#cite_note-ABC_News_August_23-3)

The brother of Soltys' murdered wife, Petro Nakonechnyi, said that even though he saw Soltys as a friend, he did not want the couple to get married because he saw Soltys as having "an unbalanced temper". After the couple married, Soltys often threatened to hang himself, Nakonechnyi said. He also said, "He beat her when she was pregnant, and once pushed her out of a car on low speed."[[1]](#cite_note-Fox_News_August_26-1)

During one violent encounter, Nakonechnyi claimed that he and his brother went to the married couple's residence and tried to take their sister back home. Soltys retaliated and tried to attack the brothers with an ax. After this incident, Soltys left Ukraine, leaving his wife and newborn son and joining his parents in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)") in 1998. After he arrived in New York, he ended up jobless after a car accident injury and was collecting [welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_spending#United_States "Welfare spending") assistance.[[1]](#cite_note-Fox_News_August_26-1)

Polina Horbonis, Soltys' Ukrainian language teacher at a local school in Shumsk, before he attended vocational training to become a shoemaker, said: "This child had such a character that you never knew what to expect from him in the next moment."[[1]](#cite_note-Fox_News_August_26-1)

## Migration

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nikolay_Soltys&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Migration")]

Shortly after his son was born, Nikolay left Ukraine and traveled to [Binghamton, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binghamton,_New_York "Binghamton, New York"), where his parents had settled in the mid-1990s. Family members say Nikolay's parents had moved to the United States under the 1989 Lautenberg Amendment to the Foreign Operations Appropriations Act, a policy that allowed refugees from [post-Soviet states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Soviet_states "Post-Soviet states") to migrate to the U.S., which included Ukraine.[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Lautenberg-5)

During this time, over 90 percent of the recent Ukrainian refugees in the United States had successfully immigrated as an outcome of the Lautenberg Amendment. The amendment required the [U.S. attorney general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._attorney_general "U.S. attorney general") to identify Evangelical Christians, Ukrainian Catholics, Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox and Jews. These identified populations of refugees were referred to as "likely targets of persecution" in the former Soviet Union. Under this legislation, candidates were permitted admission if they could prove a justifiable fear of persecution. In practice, one's admission could be granted by simply telling U.S. embassy officials that such a fear was in place.[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)

102|## Migration
103|
104|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nikolay_Soltys&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Migration")]
105|
106|Shortly after his son was born, Nikolay left Ukraine and traveled to [Binghamton, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binghamton,_New_York "Binghamton, New York"), where his parents had settled in the mid-1990s. Family members say Nikolay's parents had moved to the United States under the 1989 Lautenberg Amendment to the Foreign Operations Appropriations Act, a policy that allowed refugees from [post-Soviet states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Soviet_states "Post-Soviet states") to migrate to the U.S., which included Ukraine.[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Lautenberg-5)
107|
108|During this time, over 90 percent of the recent Ukrainian refugees in the United States had successfully immigrated as an outcome of the Lautenberg Amendment. The amendment required the [U.S. attorney general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._attorney_general "U.S. attorney general") to identify Evangelical Christians, Ukrainian Catholics, Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox and Jews. These identified populations of refugees were referred to as "likely targets of persecution" in the former Soviet Union. Under this legislation, candidates were permitted admission if they could prove a justifiable fear of persecution. In practice, one's admission could be granted by simply telling U.S. embassy officials that such a fear was in place.[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)
109|
110|In 1998, the U.S. had limited the number of Soviet refugees allowed to enter the country to 50,000. As of 1995, priority was provided to designated groups of former Soviet citizens that the U.S. Congress had recognized as probable targets for persecution. The groups included [Ukrainian Catholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_Catholics "Ukrainian Catholics"), Evangelical Christians, Jews and followers of the [Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_Autocephalous_Orthodox_Church "Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church").[[6]](#cite_note-Refugees_in_America-6)
111|
112|A requirement called for the applicant to be of "good moral character", said INS spokeswoman Kimberly Weissman, in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") "We wouldn't have approved an applicant who openly or admittedly has a criminal record," Weissman said.[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)
113|
114|Soltys was able to join his parents in 1998, using their status as persecuted Evangelical Christians, which gained his parents entry into the United States.[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)
115|
116|20-year-old Ananiy Vasyura, who defined himself as Soltys' best friend in Binghamton, New York, recalls Soltys as a "real Christian guy" who frequently recited Bible verses. He noted that Soltys didn't drink or do drugs and liked working on cars. While in New York, Soltys had little money and lost his car after an accident. The crash also left him with back pain. Vasyura said Soltys often visited a [chiropractor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiropractor "Chiropractor") after the accident and wasn't working due to his injuries.[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)
117|
118|After the loss of his father, Soltys and his mother decided to join relatives in California and moved to Sacramento. "He just thought it would be better there than here," Vasyura said. "Financially and weather-wise".[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)
119|
120|## Murders
121|
122|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nikolay_Soltys&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Murders")]
123|
124|After 9 a.m. on Monday, August 20, 2001, the killings started at three locations; two in the suburbs of Sacramento, with the third alleged to have taken place in a field in [Placer County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Placer_County,_California "Placer County, California"), adjacent to, the north of, Sacramento County.[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)
125|
126|### Pregnant wife
127|
128|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nikolay_Soltys&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Pregnant wife")]
129|
130|As Lyubov, Soltys' wife of over 3 years, was about to leave a [duplex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duplex_(building) "Duplex (building)") they had moved into two months earlier, when Soltys began stabbing her. Wounded, Lyubov tried to escape and went to their next-door neighbor's home for help. The neighbors immediately fled into their garage. The couple then listened from the garage as Soltys finished his wife's murder. According to the couple, Soltys then got into his car and sped away.[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)
131|
132|The [Sacramento County Sheriff's Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_County_Sheriff's_Department "Sacramento County Sheriff's Department") said they received a [911](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/911_(emergency_telephone_number) "911 (emergency telephone number)") call around 10 a.m. from a Scallop Court resident in [North Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Highlands,_California "North Highlands, California"). When deputies arrived, another neighbor, Vitaly Maznik, acted as an [interpreter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_interpretation "Language interpretation") for detectives. Maznik said Soltys' wife was three months pregnant and scheduled to start her new job at 9:30 a.m. Responding officers found Lyubov's body in front of her neighbor's home. "He finished her there," Maznik said. "It's a terrible story."[[7]](#cite_note-SF_Gate_21_August_Derbeken-7)[[8]](#cite_note-CNN_21_August-8)
133|
134|Before 10 a.m., Soltys left the North Highlands murder scene. Witnesses told detectives he had fled in his 1995 silver [Nissan Altima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nissan_Altima "Nissan Altima"). He drove to the home of his aunt and uncle in [Rancho Cordova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rancho_Cordova,_California "Rancho Cordova, California").[[8]](#cite_note-CNN_21_August-8)[[9]](#cite_note-SF_Gate_14_February-9)
135|
136|### Aunt, uncle and cousins
137|
138|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nikolay_Soltys&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Aunt, uncle and cousins")]
139|
140|Soltys had lived with his aunt and uncle prior to his wife's arrival from Ukraine. When he first arrived Monday morning he showed no signs of trouble, authorities said.[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)
141|
142|Before 11 a.m., authorities received a second 9-1-1 call from a neighbor down the street, who saw a girl's body in the roadway and dialed 911 to report a hit-and-run. "I thought she was run over by a car, and then I heard a woman say, 'There's another one over here,'" Christopher Smith said.[[4]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_26_August-4)
143|
144|*[The Sacramento Bee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sacramento_Bee "The Sacramento Bee")* daily newspaper reported that, according to sources, Soltys, his aunt, and uncle - went up to the second-floor of the duplex. Evidence indicates that the three had chatted politely for a while about family matters. At the closing of the discussion is when, authorities said, Soltys produced a knife and killed them. The couple were found in an upstairs bathroom.[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)
145|
146|Detectives said Soltys then went downstairs for his young cousins, who also lived on Mills Station Road. He attacked 10-year-old Dmitriy, also using a knife. This is when 9-year-old Tatyana had tried to free her cousin from Soltys' attack.[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)
147|
148|Tatyana's aunt Inna Yasinsky said that Dmitriy's mother witnessed part of the attack after hearing screams from her duplex home next door. Yasinky said, "She saw her son stabbed and her beloved niece stabbed." She said that Tatyana was killed while trying to save her cousin, and that two other children managed to escape. Tatyana's twin sister, Galina, and her little sister, Viktoria, were also targets of the killings, investigators said, but escaped by running away from the scene. Later that same day, the fathers of the two murdered children came out of their homes and started washing their children's blood from the outer walls of the duplex and walkways..[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)
149|
150|Authorities noted that Soltys left the Mills Station murder scene and drove to his mother's house in [Citrus Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citrus_Heights,_California "Citrus Heights, California"), a suburb of Sacramento, where she was babysitting his 3-year-old son Sergey Soltys. Soltys was to have enrolled in the [American River College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_River_College "American River College") in [Foothill Farms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foothill_Farms,_California "Foothill Farms, California") that same day. This directed detectives to determine the reason for why Soltys' mother was caring for the boy. His enrollment did not occur.[[7]](#cite_note-SF_Gate_21_August_Derbeken-7)[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)
151|
152|[Firefighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firefighter "Firefighter") arrived on scene first and found a severely stabbed young girl lying in the middle of the street in front of the elderly aunt and uncle's duplex. The girl was 9-year-old Tatyana Kukharskaya, their granddaughter. She was immediately taken to the [University of California at Davis Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Davis_Medical_Center "UC Davis Medical Center"), where she was pronounced dead upon arrival. A spokeswoman for the center announced that the girl had died en route to the center. A 10-year-old grandson of the elderly couple, Dmitry Kukharskiy, was found dead on the walkway adjacent to the front of the duplex. Witnesses said that the brutally stabbed children ran from their grandparents' home and the boy died in the arms of his mother, who ran out of the other half of the duplex when she heard the children screaming. The children were cousins and [second cousins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cousin "Cousin") to Soltys. His aunt and uncle - 74-year-old Galina Kukharskaya, and 75-year-old Peter Kukharskiy (the variations in the spelling of their last names distinguish gender) - were found dead on the second floor of their duplex.[[7]](#cite_note-SF_Gate_21_August_Derbeken-7)[[8]](#cite_note-CNN_21_August-8)[[11]](#cite_note-KPIX_20_August-11)
153|
154|### Son's death
155|
156|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nikolay_Soltys&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Son's death")]
157|
158|When Soltys arrived at his mother's home on Monday afternoon, she told detectives on Tuesday that he seemed peaceful but hasty. He instantly walked to the kitchen sink and washed his hands, and the mother said he seemed messy but she saw no obvious bloodstains. After washing his hands, he quickly took his 3-year-old, blonde haired son, Sergey Soltys, and left.[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)
159|
160|With multiple witnesses connecting Soltys' Nissan Altima to the Midland Heights and Rancho Cordova murder scene getaways, police were able to find the abandoned Altima in the midnight hours of Monday. Detectives discovered a photo in the abandoned car a little after midnight on Tuesday. Authorities said the photo was found tucked away in the driver's side door storage compartment. Written on the back of the photo, of Sergey Soltys being held on his mother's lap, was a clue of where his son's body could be found. The note was written in Ukrainian, Soltys' mother translated the note for law enforcement, "He is in a box on a garbage pile at the end of Watt Avenue near the tower."[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)[[12]](#cite_note-UPI_21_August-12)[[13]](#cite_note-KPIX_22_August-13)
161|
162|The boy's body was discovered in a blood-filled cardboard box, that was made for a 37-inch television set, by Sacramento County sheriff personnel. Prior to the discovery, sheriff officials had been searching along Watt Avenue, with helicopters and [K-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_dog "Police dog") units, since the early morning hours of Tuesday. "I thought there was some hope that we'd still find the kid alive," said Sacramento County Sheriff Lou Blanas after the discovery of the toddler's body was released. "It is just very sad that this is the way it turned out."[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)[[14]](#cite_note-The_World_AP_21_August-14)
163|
164|Soltys' abandoned Nissan Altima was found Monday night near the intersection of Auburn Boulevard and Madison Avenue. When detectives found the photo, they were not sure the message was authentic or simply a lie to lead the official's investigation in a flawed direction.[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)
165|
166|In the hours prior to the toddler's discovery, four Russian-speaking Sacramentans, made up of two sheriff deputies and two civilians, were the first persons to attempt to translate the photo's note. They told investigators that "The boy could be found in a box at the end of Watt avenue." Based on this translation an extensive search was conducted over hours where Watt Avenue dead ends at Baseline Road, just across the Sacramento County line in Placer County.[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)
167|
168|Officials came up empty handed in their search and the Sheriff's Department then brought Soltys' mother in for questioning and to look at the note. She found the word "tower" in the writing, officials said the initial Russian translators missed the word due to differences in their [dialects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialect#Ukraine "Dialect").[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)
169|
170|With this new information of the tower, Blanas ordered the entire department's day shift to remain on duty and to ready for the expanded search of Watt Avenue. At approximately 4 p.m., investigators discovered the cardboard box. It was found in Placer County approximately half-a-mile from the corner of Baseline Road and Crowder Lane, within a couple of miles from where Watt Avenue ended. The box was placed below a telecommunication switching tower atop a pile of garbage in a [grove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grove_(nature) "Grove (nature)") of oak trees. Authorities announced that the boy's killing appeared to be from knife stabbings and the cutting off of the child's tongue, leading him to bleed profusely from his mouth. They speculated that his life was taken on Monday afternoon, within hours of the previous family murders.[[10]](#cite_note-Sac_Bee_22_August-10)[[13]](#cite_note-KPIX_22_August-13)
171|
172|Later an auto mechanic contacted the authorities and told them he had worked on the vehicle that Soltys was driving Monday evening. He described the vehicle as a mid-1990s emerald green [Ford Explorer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Explorer "Ford Explorer") with the color silver at the bumper line and below. The mechanic said Soltys' son, Sergey, was with the suspect at the time. He said he had worked on the car around 8 p.m. and had removed cargo rails from the top of the vehicle.[[15]](#cite_note-CNN_24_August-15)[[16]](#cite_note-BBC_22_August-16)[[17]](#cite_note-KPIX_22_August_Explorer-17)
173|
174|## Aftermath
175|
176|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nikolay_Soltys&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Aftermath")]
177|
178|On August 23, he became the [466th fugitive to be placed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#2000–2003 "FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives, 2000s") on the [FBI's Ten Most Wanted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives "FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives") list. On August 30, Soltys was arrested in the backyard of a family member's home without incident in [Citrus Heights, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citrus_Heights,_California "Citrus Heights, California") and was booked into the Sacramento County Jail. He subsequently [committed suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committed_suicide "Committed suicide") by [hanging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging "Hanging") himself in his cell on February 13, 2002.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

August 30, 2001 | * FBI National Press Office   (202) 324-3691 |    Sacramento, CA -- Richard R. Baker, Special Agent in Charge (SAC) of the Sacramento Division of the FBI, U.S. Marshal Jerry Enomoto, and Sacramento County Sheriff Lou Blanas announced that earlier today FBI "Ten Most Wanted Fugitive" Nikolay Soltys was arrested in Citrus Heights, California, a suburb of Sacramento. Soltys was located in the backyard of a family member's home and taken into custody without incident by Sacramento County Sheriff's Deputies and Officers from the Sacramento Police Department. FBI Agents and Deputies from the U.S. Marshals were also on scene during the arrest. Soltys is currently being detained at the Sacramento County Jail.  Nikolay Soltys, who was being sought for the murder of six of his family members in and around the Sacramento area, was considered armed and extremely dangerous.Soltys allegedly stabbed his 23-year-old pregnant wife to death in their North Highlands, California, home on August 20, 2001. He reportedly then drove to the home of his aunt and uncle where he is suspected of killing the couple and his two young cousins. After the first five murders, Soltys allegedly drove to his mother's house and picked up his three-year-old son. On August 21, 2001, investigators located the boy's body in an empty field in Roseville, California.  A state arrest warrant for murder was issued for Nikolay Soltys on August 20, 2001, by the California Superior Court for the County of Sacramento in Sacramento, California. Then, on August 21, 2001, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of California issued a federal arrest warrant charging Soltys with unlawful flight to avoid prosecution.  Nikolay Soltys was the 466th person to be placed on the FBI's "Ten Most Wanted Fugitives" list, which began in 1950. Since then, 438 fugitives have been apprehended or located, 140 of them as a result of citizen cooperation. "The FBI is indebted to the media for keeping this case in the public eye, and to the Ukrainian community for helping to capture this dangerous fugitive," said SAC Baker.  Further information about Nikolay Soltys, including his wanted poster, is available on the FBI's Internet website.     * # FBI "Ten Most Wanted Fugitive" Nikolay Soltys Arrested in Sacramento

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Washington, D.C.  August 30, 2001 | * FBI National Press Office   (202) 324-3691 |

Sacramento, CA -- Richard R. Baker, Special Agent in Charge (SAC) of the Sacramento Division of the FBI, U.S. Marshal Jerry Enomoto, and Sacramento County Sheriff Lou Blanas announced that earlier today FBI "Ten Most Wanted Fugitive" Nikolay Soltys was arrested in Citrus Heights, California, a suburb of Sacramento. Soltys was located in the backyard of a family member's home and taken into custody without incident by Sacramento County Sheriff's Deputies and Officers from the Sacramento Police Department. FBI Agents and Deputies from the U.S. Marshals were also on scene during the arrest. Soltys is currently being detained at the Sacramento County Jail.

Nikolay Soltys, who was being sought for the murder of six of his family members in and around the Sacramento area, was considered armed and extremely dangerous.Soltys allegedly stabbed his 23-year-old pregnant wife to death in their North Highlands, California, home on August 20, 2001. He reportedly then drove to the home of his aunt and uncle where he is suspected of killing the couple and his two young cousins. After the first five murders, Soltys allegedly drove to his mother's house and picked up his three-year-old son. On August 21, 2001, investigators located the boy's body in an empty field in Roseville, California.

A state arrest warrant for murder was issued for Nikolay Soltys on August 20, 2001, by the California Superior Court for the County of Sacramento in Sacramento, California. Then, on August 21, 2001, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of California issued a federal arrest warrant charging Soltys with unlawful flight to avoid prosecution.

Nikolay Soltys was the 466th person to be placed on the FBI's "Ten Most Wanted Fugitives" list, which began in 1950. Since then, 438 fugitives have been apprehended or located, 140 of them as a result of citizen cooperation. "The FBI is indebted to the media for keeping this case in the public eye, and to the Ukrainian community for helping to capture this dangerous fugitive," said SAC Baker.

Further information about Nikolay Soltys, including his wanted poster, is available on the FBI's Internet website.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 4: Seal of the Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Seal_of_the_Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation.svg/250px-Seal_of_the_Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seal_of_the_Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation.svg)

The **FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives during the 2000s** is a list, maintained for a sixth decade, of the [Ten Most Wanted Fugitives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives "FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives") of the United States [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation"). At any given time, the FBI is actively searching for 12,000 fugitives. During the 2000s, 36 new fugitives were added to the list. By the close of the decade a total of 494 fugitives had been listed on the Top Ten list, of whom 463 have been captured or located.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-Mueller-1)

## FBI headlines in the 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: FBI headlines in the 2000s")]

The 2000s (decade) started out badly for the FBI's much needed attempts to upgrade technology. First, the "Trilogy" project went far over the $380 million budget, and behind its three-year schedule. Then, [Virtual Case File](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Case_File "Virtual Case File") (VCF) planned for completion in 2003, was officially abandoned in 2005, after more than $100 million spent.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-2) A new, more ambitious investigation software project, Sentinel, was introduced in 2005 as a replacement for the failed VCF system.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-3)

In 2001, [Robert Hanssen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hanssen "Robert Hanssen"), high within the Bureau, was caught selling information to the [Russians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), and Bureau security practices came into question.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-4)

In 2002 the FBI's official top priority became [counter-terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-terrorism "Counter-terrorism"), followed second by counterintelligence. The [USA PATRIOT Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_PATRIOT_Act "USA PATRIOT Act") granted the FBI increased monitoring powers.

157|## FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives to begin the 2000s
158|
159|[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives to begin the 2000s")]

161|The FBI in the past has identified individuals by the sequence number in which each individual has appeared on the list. Some individuals have even appeared twice, and often a sequence number was permanently assigned to an individual suspect who was soon caught, captured, or simply removed, before his or her appearance could be published on the publicly released list. In those cases, the public would see only gaps in the number sequence reported by the FBI. For convenient reference, the wanted suspect's sequence number and date of entry on the FBI list appear below, whenever possible.
162|
163|The following [fugitives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fugitive "Fugitive") made up the top Ten list to begin the 2000s:

Later he escaped from Mexican prison September 1991 after murdering a prison inmate in April 1991.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-10) As of May 19, 2016, he was no longer on the list. |

194|Brown, 33, who had homes at both Canterbury and Lilliput in St James, was killed during a running gun battle with the police in Barrett Town, Montego Bay.
195|
196|Assistant Superintendent of Police Dave Hyman said the police went on an operation in Barrett Town, where they came under heavy gunfire from a group of gunmen. The gunfire, he said, lasted for a “number of minutes” during which a member of the police team, Sydney Brevett, was grazed on the arm by a bullet from gunman’s weapon.
197|
198|Following the shooting, Brown was found suffering from bullet wounds and was taken to the Cornwall Regional Hospital where he was pronounced dead.
199|
200|Police said one of the gunmen was held and taken into custody, while another escaped.
201|
202|Two guns, according to the police, were taken from Brown’s body. One of the guns, a Carbon 15 pistol, was loaded with 15 rounds of .56 bullets. The other, a Colt .45 pistol, had five live rounds.
203|
204|Three motor cars – a silver Honda, licensed 2574 DN; a silver Toyota Corolla, registered 3490 DX, and a white Toyota Corolla, licensed 8527 EB, which the police theorised to be stolen by the men, were removed from the premises.
205|
206|A mask was also found at the premises.
207|
208|The police believe Brown, just hours before his death, was among five armed men who shot and killed Romaine Salmon, and shot and injured Nicholas Chin and Christopher Roberts in Barrett Town, a neighboring community to Liliput.
209|
210|The three were sitting on a wall during a dance in Barrett Town when the five men approached them, and began to harass one the three men, forcing Salmon to intervene, said a police spokesman.
211|
212|He said the armed men then opened fire hitting all three men, killing Salmon on the spot. The other two were also hit and were taken to hospital where they were admitted in serious, but stable condition.
213|
214|Brown, the police said yesterday, also went by the aliases Anthony Brisco, Simon Plested, Devon Foster, Eric Brown, Omar Brown, Richard Omar Kennedy, Sandokam, Sando and Shawn.
215|
216|Superintendent John Morris, the crime chief for Area One, said he was wanted by the FBI for drug trafficking, murder and conspiracy to murder.
217|
218|The Jamaican police also wanted Brown for a number of crimes including a 2001 double murder in Mt Salem.
219|
220|In addition, the police said Brown was involved in a power struggle in Canterbury with another St James wanted man, resulting in several murders in that community.

**Hopeton Eric Brown** (September 26, 1974/August 26, 1974 – March 21, 2004) was sought in the United States for his involvement in drug-related activities, as well as for the murder of a man and the attempted murder of a woman at an apartment in Saint Paul, Minnesota, on March 21, 1997. He was also wanted by authorities in Jamaica for allegedly committing two murders in Montego Bay, having killed one individual by a stray bullet and another individual for leaning on his car January 14, 2001. He was then placed on the FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives in 2001. On March 21, 2004, Brown was killed during a gunfight with Jamaican law enforcement in Barrett Town, Montego Bay, Jamaica.

**Hopeton Eric Brown** (September 26, 1974/August 26, 1974 – March 21, 2004) was sought in the United States for his involvement in drug-related activities, as well as for the murder of a man and the attempted murder of a woman at an apartment in Saint Paul, Minnesota, on March 21, 1997. He was also wanted by authorities in Jamaica for allegedly committing two murders in Montego Bay, having killed one individual by a stray bullet and another individual for leaning on his car January 14, 2001. He was then placed on the FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives in 2001. On March 21, 2004, Brown was killed during a gunfight with Jamaican law enforcement in Barrett Town, Montego Bay, Jamaica.

# Jury chooses life, not death, for killer of 2

### Share this:

After nearly eight years of waiting for justice, families of two employees shot to death during a robbery at an Orlando U-Haul business learned Tuesday that the killer would spend the rest of his life in prison.

By one vote, a jury spared the life of Aurlieas Dane McClarty, 30, who shot to death Phillip D. Mumaw, 59, and Anne Culp, 48, during a robbery on July 18, 2000.

“This is not the verdict that I had hoped for, but I think ultimately we won anyway,” said Sheila DiGregorio, one of Mumaw’s five children and two stepchildren, who attended along with his widow. “As long as he can’t walk the streets, I can live with it.”

McClarty stood silently, hands and legs shackled, as a clerk read the jury’s recommendation. The five-man, seven-woman jury deliberated about 90 minutes before recommending by the slimmest margin — 6-6 — that McClarty spend his life in prison. The only other option was the death penalty, which the state sought.

Orange Circuit Judge Bob Wattles immediately sentenced McClarty to two consecutive life terms. After an eight-day trial, McClarty was convicted May 7 of two counts of first-degree murder and robbery with a firearm. The judge also gave him nearly 21 years for the robbery count, to be served at the same time as the life sentences.

McClarty shot Mumaw, the store manager, and Culp with a .380-caliber Colt pistol as they stood behind a cash register. He escaped with $200. His history includes an arson conviction in Oklahoma for throwing a Molotov cocktail into an occupied home, and a conviction for bank robbery in Maryland, Assistant State Attorney Linda Drane Burdick said. She would not comment on the sentencing.

During the penalty phase of the trial, which began Monday, the defense argued that McClarty was mentally ill, so he should not have to pay for his crimes with his life. The judge found McClarty incompetent to stand trial in 2003, postponing his first trial after a jury had been selected, and he was sent to a state mental hospital.

McClarty’s mother and stepfather, Sandra and Melvin Johnson of Oklahoma, testified that he had been hospitalized at least nine times, starting when he was 11 or 12 years old. He also has a history of suicide attempts, including one in which he drank bleach.

Francis Iennaco, one of two court-appointed defense attorneys, said he would appeal the conviction but was nonetheless “thrilled” by the jury’s recommendation. “He’s very seriously mentally ill and probably should have been institutionalized a long time ago,” Iennaco said.

Virginia Culp, Anne Culp’s sister-in-law, said the family is relieved the long ordeal is over. Anne Culp, a former social worker, had six children.

“He’s never going to see the light of day again, so he can never hurt another family,” Virginia Culp said from her home in Illinois. “That’s what matters to us. If he’s got anything more coming, God is going to take care of it.”

# Guilty verdict in U-Haul killings

### Share this:

* [Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook](https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2008/05/08/guilty-verdict-in-u-haul-killings/?share=facebook)

By

PUBLISHED: | UPDATED:

**Getting your [Trinity Audio](//trinityaudio.ai) player ready...**

Phillip Mumaw’s family waited eight years to hear a guilty verdict.

And it took an Orange County jury less than three hours to deliver it.

On Wednesday, jurors found 30-year-old Aurlieas Dane McClarty guilty of two counts of first-degree murder and robbery with a firearm.

Prosecutors say McClarty walked into an Orlando U-haul store with a .380-caliber Colt pistol in the early morning of July 18, 2000.

He shot 59-year-old Mumaw, the store’s manager, and 48-year-old Anne Culp, an employee, as they stood behind a register.

McClarty stole $200 and fled.

More than a dozen relatives of Mumaw sat through the eight-day trial. They held back tears through some testimony and comforted one another outside the courtroom when times got hard. Culp’s family did not attend.

“My father was a very loving man,” said Mumaw’s oldest son, Steve Mumaw, 44. “We’ve been trying to deal with it the best way we could because it’s been a very difficult situation.”

The penalty phase will begin Monday at 9 a.m. That’s when attorneys on both sides will present evidence as to why McClarty should or should not be executed by the state.

The same jurors who found him guilty will make a recommendation — either life in prison or death — to Orange Circuit Court Judge Bob Wattles. The judge will make the final determination at a later date.

This is the second trial for McClarty.

In 2003, a jury was selected and testimony was starting when the judge postponed the trial. At that time, doctors found McClarty to be incompetent to stand trial.

He was sent to a state mental hospital for treatment. Nearly four years later, Wattles found him competent to stand trial.

McClarty showed little emotion Wednesday when the verdict was read. He stood next to his two defense attorneys with his wrists and ankles shackled. More than a dozen deputies and corrections officers filled the courtroom in case McClarty acted up. He remained calm.

As deputies escorted McClarty out of the courtroom, some of Mumaw’s family members hugged prosecutor Linda Drane-Burdick. Orlando police Detective Joel Wright — who helped investigate the case with now-retired Detective Glen Gause — stayed to see the outcome.

“Whenever you have two people who get up in the morning and go to work and they expect their day to go as usual and then something like this happens,” he said, “it does something to you as a detective.”

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 4: Seal of the Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Seal_of_the_Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation.svg/250px-Seal_of_the_Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seal_of_the_Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation.svg)

The **FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives during the 2000s** is a list, maintained for a sixth decade, of the [Ten Most Wanted Fugitives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives "FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives") of the United States [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation"). At any given time, the FBI is actively searching for 12,000 fugitives. During the 2000s, 36 new fugitives were added to the list. By the close of the decade a total of 494 fugitives had been listed on the Top Ten list, of whom 463 have been captured or located.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-Mueller-1)

## FBI headlines in the 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: FBI headlines in the 2000s")]

The 2000s (decade) started out badly for the FBI's much needed attempts to upgrade technology. First, the "Trilogy" project went far over the $380 million budget, and behind its three-year schedule. Then, [Virtual Case File](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Case_File "Virtual Case File") (VCF) planned for completion in 2003, was officially abandoned in 2005, after more than $100 million spent.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-2) A new, more ambitious investigation software project, Sentinel, was introduced in 2005 as a replacement for the failed VCF system.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-3)

In 2001, [Robert Hanssen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hanssen "Robert Hanssen"), high within the Bureau, was caught selling information to the [Russians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), and Bureau security practices came into question.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-4)

In 2002 the FBI's official top priority became [counter-terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-terrorism "Counter-terrorism"), followed second by counterintelligence. The [USA PATRIOT Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_PATRIOT_Act "USA PATRIOT Act") granted the FBI increased monitoring powers.
